results.key_findings: Five regions for dissemination in space (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve); kFLC index accepted as an alternative to CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands; central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting MRI markers; additional supporting evidence recommended in people over 50 or with vascular risk factors.

results.key_findings: NMOSD with AQP4-IgG requires one core clinical characteristic (optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, acute brainstem, diencephalic or cerebral syndrome) and a positive cell-based AQP4-IgG assay; seronegative NMOSD requires additional clinical and MRI criteria.

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not treat heat-triggered transient blurring (Uhthoff phenomenon) as a new relapse requiring further steroids
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria: two attacks (right optic neuritis 8 months ago with residual pallor, current left T9-T10 myelitis) and DIS in four MRI regions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord), with enhancing and non-enhancing lesions

Treat the myelitis relapse, which limits walking, with methylprednisolone oral 500 mg daily for 5 days or IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days, after a urine dipstick excludes infection (she has urinary urgency); stop ibuprofen during the course and consider a proton pump inhibitor; plasma exchange if a disabling relapse does not respond
Assess the urinary urgency with a post-void residual: an antimuscarinic if the residual is low, intermittent self-catheterisation if it is raised
Explain that heat-triggered transient blurring and leg heaviness (Uhthoff phenomenon) are not new relapses, and advise cooling

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (two attacks in 8 months, enhancing brain and thoracic cord lesions), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception
Before an anti-CD20 or S1P modulator, check HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV antibody and VZV IgG (HIV already non-reactive) and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Wei Chen is a 27-year-old right-handed East Asian woman who presents with a 10-day history of progressive weakness and numbness in her left lower extremity accompanied by gait unsteadiness. She first noticed a tingling sensation in her left foot approximately two weeks ago while studying, which she initially attributed to prolonged sitting. Over the following several days, the numbness ascended to involve her entire left lower leg up to the knee, and she began to notice a tight, band-like sensation around her lower chest on the left side. Concurrently, she developed progressive weakness in her left leg, manifesting as difficulty climbing stairs, a tendency for her left foot to catch on uneven surfaces, and a sense that her leg was stiff and heavy. By the time of presentation she was having difficulty walking more than a block without stumbling and felt unsafe on stairs. She also reports that for the past several days she has noticed worsening of her symptoms after taking hot showers, with increased leg heaviness and blurred vision in the right eye that resolves after cooling down. On further questioning, she recalls an episode approximately eight months ago when she experienced painful vision loss in her right eye over several days, which was diagnosed as optic neuritis by her ophthalmologist and treated with a short course of oral prednisone. Her vision recovered over about four weeks, though she notes that colors still appear slightly washed out in the right eye compared to the left. She additionally reports persistent fatigue over the past several months that is disproportionate to her activity level and has affected her academic performance. She has noticed occasional urinary urgency, needing to rush to the bathroom more frequently than before, but denies frank incontinence. She denies fevers, weight loss, rash, joint pain, oral ulcers, dysphagia, or recent infections. She has no history of travel outside of her home city in the past year and denies any tick bites or exposure to animals.
